label: prop: runstablecollisionpoints
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: runstablecollisionpoints}
    Under the assumptions of Prop. \ref{prop: relax max principle}, a collision is unstable under the unweighted particle gradient flow.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Following ideas used for collision singularities in Prony systems \citep{batenkov2013geometrysingularitiespronymapping} and exponential least-squares approximation \citep{1f9723a1-a04e-3d21-9c1b-61527608e570}, a pair of colliding kernel functions can be replaced by a divided-difference basis.
 
This remains non-degenerate at the collision and converges to a kernel derivative.
 
Smoothness of an ETP kernel gives the required continuity of $\Delta''$; Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle} then implies that separating the particles is unstable.

label: prop: posweightrelaxed
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: posweightrelaxed}
Suppose $k$ is real, analytic, and universal, or that $k$ is ETP and the problem is well specified.
 
Then, at any nonzero local minimum of $\bar F$, every weight vector $\mathbf w$ attaining the minimum in \eqref{eq:relaxed-objective} satisfies $w_i\neq0$ for all $i=1,\ldots,N$.
 
Moreover, the particle locations are distinct.
head: environment

label: thm: relaxbound
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider a nonzero local minimum.
 
By Prop.~\ref{prop: posweightrelaxed}, all particle locations are distinct and every optimal weight is nonzero.
 
Hence stationarity forces a double zero of $\Delta$ at each of the $N$ particle locations.
 
Since $\Delta$ is a nonzero combination of at most $N+K$ distinct kernel sections, extended total positivity implies that it has at most $N+K-1$ zeros counting multiplicity.
 
Thus $2N\leq N+K-1$, which requires $N\leq K-1$.
 
Therefore, when $N\geq K$, every local minimum must satisfy $\bar F=0$.

Now consider a spurious stationary point.
 
If all particle locations are distinct, Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle} implies that every location is active, so the same zero-counting argument again gives a contradiction when $N\geq K$.
 
Hence every spurious stationary point must contain a collision, which is unstable by Prop.~\ref{prop: runstablecollisionpoints}.
head: environment

label: thm: relaxepsbound
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This result is also proved via a zero counting argument.
 
First, the maximum principle (cf. Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle}) confines the active particles to the convex hull of the target support.
 
Meanwhile, compactness and analyticity give an upper bound on the number of distinct active locations that a stationary witness with $\operatorname{MMD}(P,P^*)\geq\varepsilon$ can support, depending only on $D$ and $\varepsilon$.
 
At a nonzero local minimum, all $N$ particle locations must be distinct (cf. Prop.~\ref{prop: posweightrelaxed}), yielding a contradiction once $N$ exceeds this bound.
 
Meanwhile, for a general stationary point, exceeding the bound forces a collision, which must be unstable (cf. Prop.~\ref{prop: runstablecollisionpoints}).

label: thm: SimpBound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: SimpBound}
Suppose the problem is well specified.
 
There exists a finite threshold $N(P^*)$ such that, whenever $N>N(P^*)$, $F$ has no spurious local minima over $\mathbf w\in\Delta^{N-1}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb R^N$.
 
Moreover, every spurious stationary point is unstable under the unweighted particle gradient flow.

label: prop: Hinterp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: Hinterp}
Let $\bar{x}_1,\ldots,\bar{x}_K$ and $x_1^*,\ldots,x_K^*$ each consist of distinct real numbers.
 
Define 
\begin{equation}
    H(\cdot)
=
\sum_{i=1}^K
\left[
\alpha_i k(\cdot,\bar{x}_i)
+
\beta_i\partial_2k(\cdot,\bar{x}_i)
\right].
\end{equation}
Then there exist $\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta$ such that $H(x)<1$ for all $x\notin\{x_1^*,\ldots,x_K^*\}$, and 
\begin{align*}
    H(x_i^*)=1, \qquad H'(x_i^*)=0 \qquad i=1,\ldots,K.
\end{align*}

label: prop: simp max principle
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: simp max principle}
Suppose $(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})$ is a stationary point of $F$ with $F(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})>0$, with weights constrained to the simplex.
 
Suppose also that $k$ is ETP, translation invariant, and normalisable, and that $c\geq0$.
 
Then $\Delta(x)\leq c$ for all $x$, every distinct particle location is active, and for every $i=1,\dots,N$,
 
\begin{equation*}
    \Delta(x_i)=c,
    \qquad
    \Delta'(x_i)=0,
    \qquad
    \Delta''(x_i)<0.
\end{equation*}

label: prop: unstablecollisionpoints
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: unstablecollisionpoints}
Under the assumptions of Prop.~\ref{prop: simp max principle}, every collision is unstable under the unweighted particle gradient flow.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Separate two colliding particles by a small distance $r=x_j-x_i$.
 
Under the unweighted particle flow,
 
$
    \dot r
    =
    -\bigl(\Delta'(x_j)-\Delta'(x_i)\bigr)
    =
    -\Delta''(\vartheta)r
$
 
for some $\vartheta\in(x_i,x_j)$ by the mean value theorem.
 
Since $\Delta''<0$ in a neighbourhood of the collision, $\dot r$ has the same sign as $r$.
 
Thus the collision is unstable.

label: prop: collisionpoints
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: collisionpoints}
Under the assumptions of Prop.~\ref{prop: simp max principle}, a collision is not a local minimum.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $x_i = x_j$, and $w_i, w_j > 0$.
     
    Perturb the locations to
     
    $x_i - \frac{w_j}{w_i + w_j}\varepsilon$ and $x_j + \frac{w_i}{w_i + w_j}\varepsilon$.
     
    If $F(\varepsilon)$ denotes the perturbed objective, then
     
    \begin{equation*}
        F(\varepsilon)-F(0)
        =
        \frac{w_iw_j}{w_i+w_j}\Delta''(x_j)\varepsilon^2+o(\varepsilon^2)<0,
    \end{equation*}
     
    for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$.
     
    Thus, the perturbation decreases the objective for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$.
     
    If one of the weights is zero, transfer an arbitrarily small amount of mass to that particle without changing the measure, then apply the same perturbation.

\label{prop: Lcbound}
Suppose $P^*$ has compact support of diameter at most $D$, and $(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})$ is a stationary point with $F(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})>0$.
 
Then
 
\begin{align*}
    \|\Delta\|_1
    \leq&
    2(\sqrt{2}+D)c
    +16c\sqrt{-\log c}\\
    &+
    6\sqrt{\pi}\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt{-\log c})
    +
    4\sqrt{\pi}c\sqrt{1-2\log c}.
\end{align*}

title: Proof
body_md:
Split the real line into regions near the target support, intermediate regions, and Gaussian tails.
 
The maximum principle controls the witness directly on the central region; the tails are bounded using Gaussian decay.
 
The main difficulty is to remove any dependence on how far the extreme particles lie from the target.
 
We do this using the stationarity equations at the extreme particles to obtain probability-mass bounds, after which suitable choices of the splitting points yield the stated uniform estimate.

title: Proof
body_md:
The maximum principle gives a lower bound on the probability mass in a neighbourhood of each particle.
 
We group overlapping neighbourhoods into connected components and construct a maximal separated packing in each component.
 
This controls the component diameters and hence, by Jensen-type zero counting for the shifted witness function $\Delta-c$, the number of double zeros contributed by the particles.
 
Summing over components gives the stated bound.

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a function $K: [a,b] \times [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ which is continuously differentiable as needed, and given a sequence of points $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ such that $a \le x_1 \le\ldots \le  x_n \le b$, let the sequence $m_1, \ldots, m_n$ be defined in \eqref{msequenceforet}.
     
    Let the functions $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n$ be defined by the formula
     
    $
    \phi_j(t) = \frac{\partial^{m_j}K}{\partial x^{m_j}}(x_j, t).
    $
     
    Then $K$ is ETP if $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n$ form an extended Chebyshev system on $[c, d]$ for all such sequences of $x_i$.

title: Proposition

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by defining the reduced measure of $P$ by merging particles at the same location, and removing locations with zero total weight.
     
    Write $\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_A$ for its distinct locations and $\varsigma_1,\ldots,\varsigma_A$ for their nonzero total weights.
     
    By the stationarity conditions, we have
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta(\vartheta_j)=0, \qquad \Delta'(\vartheta_j)=0, \qquad j=1,\ldots,A.
    \end{equation*}
     
    To apply the variation diminishing property, write
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta(x)=\int k(t,x)g(t)\,\mathrm d\sigma(t), \qquad g=\frac{\mathrm d(P-P^*)}{\mathrm d\sigma}, \qquad \sigma=|P|+P^*.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Since the positive part of $g$ is supported on at most $A$ distinct locations, we must have $V(g)\leq 2A$.
     
    Moreover, since $\bar F(\boldsymbol{x})>0$, the witness $\Delta$ is not identically zero.
     
    The variation diminishing property (cf. Def.~\ref{def: Variation deimishing}) therefore gives $Z(\Delta)\leq V(g)$, where zeros are counted with multiplicity.
     
    On the other hand, the stationarity conditions imply that each $\vartheta_j$ is a zero of multiplicity at least two.
     
    Consequently,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        2A\leq Z(\Delta)\leq V(g)\leq 2A.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Thus all inequalities are equalities, and the $\vartheta_j$ are the only zeros of $\Delta$, each with multiplicity exactly two.
     
    Since the positive part of $g$ is supported on at most $A$ locations, equality $V(g)=2A$ requires the alternating sign pattern negative--positive--negative--$\cdots$--positive--negative.
     
    Thus every location in the reduced measure must have strictly positive total weight.
     
    Moreover, since the negative contributions outside the positive locations must arise from $P^*$, these locations lie within the convex hull of $\operatorname{supp}(P^*)$.
     

    We next establish that $\Delta\leq0$.
     
    Since all zeros of $\Delta$ have multiplicity exactly two, $\Delta$ cannot change sign.
     
    Furthermore, the weight optimality conditions give $\int\Delta\,\mathrm dP=0$, and hence
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \int\Delta\,\mathrm dP^*=-\int\Delta\,\mathrm d(P-P^*)=-\|\Delta\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2<0.
    \end{equation*}
     
    It follows that $\Delta\leq0$ everywhere.
     
    Finally, weight optimality gives $\Delta(x_i)=0$ for every particle, including those with zero individual weight.
     
    Since all zeros of $\Delta$ occur at the active locations $\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_A$, every particle must coincide with one of these locations.
     
    Thus every distinct particle location is active, has positive total weight, and lies within the convex hull of $\operatorname{supp}(P^*)$.
     
    Moreover, each particle location is a strict local maximum of $\Delta$, and its zero has multiplicity exactly two.
     
    Consequently, for every $i=1,\ldots,N$,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta'(x_i)=0, \qquad \Delta''(x_i)<0. \qedhere
    \end{equation*}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $w_i=0$.
     
    Since we are considering a local minimum with $\bar F(\boldsymbol{x})>0$, we have $\|\Delta\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2=\bar F(\boldsymbol{x})>0$.
     
    Thus, $\Delta$ is not identically zero.
     
    It follows that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists an $x'$ in an $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $x_i$ such that $x'\neq x_j$ for all $j=1,\ldots,N$ and $\Delta(x')\neq0$.
     
    This follows from analyticity when the kernel is analytic; alternatively, when the kernel is ETP and the problem is well specified, $\Delta$ is a nonzero linear combination of finitely many kernel sections and therefore has only finitely many zeros.
     
    
    Fix such a point $x'$.
     
    Since $w_i=0$, moving the $i$th particle to $x'$ leaves the measure unchanged if its weight remains zero.
     
    Reoptimising the weights at the new configuration can only decrease the objective relative to keeping the other weights fixed and optimising only the weight of the moved particle.
     
    Thus, using the reproducing property, we have that
     
    \begin{align*}
        \bar F(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1},x',x_{i+1},\ldots,x_N) &\leq \min_{w_i'\in\mathbb R}\|\Delta+w_i'k(x',\cdot)\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2\\
        &=\bar F(\boldsymbol{x})+\min_{w_i'\in\mathbb R}\left\{2w_i'\Delta(x')+(w_i')^2k(x',x')\right\}\\
        &=\bar F(\boldsymbol{x})-\frac{\Delta(x')^2}{k(x',x')} <\bar F(\boldsymbol{x}).
    \end{align*}
     
    Since $x'$ can be chosen arbitrarily close to $x_i$, this contradicts local minimality.
     
    Finally, suppose two particle locations coincide, say $x_i=x_j$.
     
    We can then transfer the weight of particle $i$ to particle $j$, setting $w_j\leftarrow w_j+w_i$ and $w_i\leftarrow0$, without changing the measure or the objective.
     
    This yields an optimal weight vector with a zero entry, contradicting the preceding argument.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the reduced measure as in the proof of Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle}.
     
    Without loss of generality, suppose the collision occurs at $\vartheta_1$.
     
    Consider perturbing some, but not all, of the particles positioned at $\vartheta_1$ to $\vartheta_1+d$, for sufficiently small $d>0$.
     
    Suppose the resulting locations $(\vartheta_1+d,\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_A)$ have weights $(\varsigma_0^d,\ldots,\varsigma_A^d)$.
     
    Then
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta_d(x) = \varsigma^d_0 k(\vartheta_1 + d, x) + \varsigma^d_1 k(\vartheta_1, x) + \sum_{i=2}^A \varsigma^d_i k(\vartheta_i, x) - \mu_{P^*}(x).
    \end{equation*}
     
    Following \citet{batenkov2013geometrysingularitiespronymapping} and \citet{1f9723a1-a04e-3d21-9c1b-61527608e570}, introduce the basis functions $\phi^d_i(\cdot)=k(\vartheta_i,\cdot)$ for $i=1,\ldots,A$, together with $\phi^d_0=\frac{k(\vartheta_1+d,\cdot)-k(\vartheta_1,\cdot)}{d}$.
     
    Define $b^d_0=\frac{\mu_{P^*}(\vartheta_1+d)-\mu_{P^*}(\vartheta_1)}{d}$, and set $b^d_i=\mu_{P^*}(\vartheta_i)$ for $i=1,\ldots,A$.
     
    We can then write
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta_d(x) = d\varsigma^d_0 \phi^d_0(x) + (\varsigma^d_0 + \varsigma^d_1)\phi_1^d(x) + \sum_{i=2}^A \varsigma^d_i \phi^d_i(x) - \mu_{P^*}(x).
    \end{equation*}
     
    Now define
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathbf{v}^d = \begin{bmatrix} d\varsigma_0^d\\ \varsigma^d_0 + \varsigma^d_1\\ \varsigma_2^d\\ \vdots\\ \varsigma_A^d \end{bmatrix}.
    \end{equation*}
     
    This is an equivalent representation of the optimised weights.
     
    For $d>0$, the map between $\mathbf v^d$ and $\boldsymbol{\varsigma}^d$ is invertible, so optimising either gives the same result.
     
    Define the matrix $K^d$ by $K^d_{ij}=\langle\phi^d_i,\phi^d_j\rangle_\mathcal{H}$.
     
    By optimality of the weights, we have $\Delta_d(\vartheta_1+d)=0$ and $\Delta_d(\vartheta_i)=0$ for $i=1,\ldots,A$.
     
    Consequently,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        K^d\mathbf{v}^d-\mathbf{b}^d = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\Delta_d(\vartheta_1+d)-\Delta_d(\vartheta_1)}{d}\\ \Delta_d(\vartheta_1)\\ \vdots\\ \Delta_d(\vartheta_A) \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0}.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Define the limiting basis by $\phi_0^0=\partial_1k(\vartheta_1,\cdot)$, with the remaining basis functions unchanged.
     
    This also defines $K^0$ and $\mathbf{b}^0$.
     
    Since $k$ is ETP, it has the smoothness required here, and hence $K^d\to K^0$ and $\mathbf b^d\to\mathbf b^0$ as $d\to0$.
     
    In this limiting basis, $(0,\boldsymbol{\varsigma})^\top$ represents the original reduced measure, and the reproducing property gives
     
    \begin{equation*}
        K^0(0,\boldsymbol{\varsigma})^\top-\mathbf{b}^0 = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta'(\vartheta_1)\\ \Delta(\vartheta_1)\\ \vdots\\ \Delta(\vartheta_A) \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{0},
    \end{equation*}
     
    where the final equality follows from stationarity at the original configuration.
     
    Since $K^0$ is invertible by the ETP property, $K^d$ is also invertible for sufficiently small $d$, and hence $\mathbf{v}^d=(K^d)^{-1}\mathbf{b}^d\to(0,\boldsymbol{\varsigma})^\top$ as $d\to0$.

    We next establish continuity of the basis functions and their derivatives as $d\to0$.
     
    Following \citet{baxter2010functionalsexponentialbrownianmotion}, observe that
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \phi_0^d(x) = \int_0^1 \partial_1k(\vartheta_1+td,x)\,\mathrm dt.
    \end{equation*}
     
    By smoothness of the kernel, we can differentiate under the integral to obtain
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \partial_x^n\phi_0^d(x) = \int_0^1 \partial_x^n\partial_1k(\vartheta_1+td,x)\,\mathrm dt.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Since the integrand is continuous in the relevant arguments, these derivatives extend continuously to $d=0$.
     
    The remaining basis functions are independent of $d$.
     
    It follows that
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta_d''(x) = \sum_{i=0}^A v_i^d\partial_x^2\phi_i^d(x)-\mu_{P^*}''(x) \to \Delta''(x),
    \end{equation*}
     
    and the extension defined by $\Delta_0''(x)=\Delta''(x)$ is jointly continuous in $d$ and $x$.
     
    This provides the continuity needed for the instability argument.
     
    Finally, by the mean value theorem,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \dot d = -\bigl(\Delta_d'(\vartheta_1+d)-\Delta_d'(\vartheta_1)\bigr) = -\Delta_d''(\varrho)d,
    \end{equation*}
     
    for some $\varrho\in(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_1+d)$.
     
    By continuity, $\Delta_d''(\varrho)<0$ in a sufficiently small neighbourhood of the stationary configuration along the perturbation considered above.
     
    Thus $\dot d$ has the same sign as $d$, establishing instability of the collision.
     
    Note, in particular, that any collided particles remain collided under the flow.
     
    Thus,  along the perturbation we retain the negativity when the other particles change positions too, and for a sufficiently small neighbourhood no other collisions occur.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a target distribution $P^*$ with compact support in $[A,B]$, where $B-A\le D$.
     
    By Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle}, all particle locations lie within this interval and have positive total weight.
     
    Moreover, if $\operatorname{MMD}\ge\varepsilon$, then there exists $x_0\in[A,B]$ such that $|\Delta(x_0)|\ge\varepsilon^2$.
     
    Indeed, stationarity gives $\int\Delta(x)\,\mathrm dP(x)=0$, and hence $\varepsilon^2\le\operatorname{MMD}^2=-\int\Delta(x)\,\mathrm dP^*(x)$.
     
    The claim then follows since $P^*$ is a probability measure.

    We next bound the analytic continuation of $\Delta$ to the complex plane, centred at $x_0$, following the approach of \citet[Lemma 4.3]{gröchenig2018sharpresultssamplingderivatives}.
     
    By Prop.~\ref{prop: relax max principle}, $P=|P|$, and hence $|P-P^*|\le P+P^*$.
     
    Moreover, by the same proposition we have $\Delta=\mu_P-\mu_{P^*}\le0$, so $\mu_P\le\mu_{P^*}\le1$, since $P^*$ is a probability measure and the kernel is bounded above by one.
     
    It follows that,
     
    \begin{align*}
        |\Delta(x_0+x+iy)| &= \left|\int e^{-(x_0+x+iy-t)^2}\,\mathrm d(P-P^*)(t)\right|\\
        &\le e^{y^2}\int e^{-(x_0+x-t)^2}\,\mathrm d(P+P^*)(t)
        \le e^{y^2}\bigl(\mu_P(x+x_0)+\mu_{P^*}(x+x_0)\bigr)\le 2e^{y^2}.
    \end{align*}
     
    We can therefore apply Prop.~\ref{prop: jenzerocount} with $f=\Delta(\cdot+x_0)$, $A_f=2$, and $B_f=1$.
     
    In particular, since each distinct particle location contributes at least two zeros, counted with multiplicity, we obtain
     
    \begin{equation*}
        N' \le \frac{\log(\frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}) + \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 (B-A)^2}{2\log(\delta)} \le \frac{\log(\frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}) + \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 D^2}{2\log(\delta)},
    \end{equation*}
     
    where $N'$ denotes the number of distinct particle locations.
     
    If $N$ exceeds this bound, then at least two particles must share a location.
     
    By Props.~\ref{prop: runstablecollisionpoints} and~\ref{prop: posweightrelaxed}, such configurations cannot be local minima and are unstable under the unweighted particle gradient flow.

body_md:
As before, we begin by defining the reduced measure of $P$ by merging particles at the same location and removing locations with zero total weight.
     
    Write $\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_A$ for its distinct locations and $\varsigma_1,\ldots,\varsigma_A$ for their nonzero total weights.
     
    By the stationarity conditions, we have that
     
    \begin{align}
        \Delta(\vartheta_j)=c, \qquad \Delta'(\vartheta_j)=0, \qquad j=1,\ldots,A.
    \end{align}
     
    Let $h=\Delta-c$. 
     
    To apply the variation diminishing property to this function, we first represent the constant $c$ as a kernel integral using translation invariance and normalisability.
     
    Let $\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure and $\mathcal Z=\int_{\mathbb R}k(t,x)\,\mathrm dt$, which is finite, positive, and independent of $x$.
     
    If $c=0$, write
     
    \begin{equation*}
        h(x)=\int k(t,x)g(t)\,\mathrm d\sigma(t), \qquad g=\frac{\mathrm d(P-P^*)}{\mathrm d\sigma}, \qquad \sigma=|P|+P^*.
    \end{equation*}
     
    If $c>0$, instead write
     
    \begin{equation*}
        h(x)=\int k(t,x)g(t)\,\mathrm d\sigma(t), \qquad g=\frac{\mathrm d(P-P^*-\frac{c}{\mathcal Z}\lambda)}{\mathrm d\sigma}, \qquad \sigma=|P|+P^*+\lambda.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Since the positive part of $g$ is supported on at most $A$ distinct locations, we must have $V(g)\leq 2A$.
     
    Moreover, since $F(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})>0$ and $P,P^*$ have equal mass, we have that $\int h\,\mathrm d(P-P^*)=\|\Delta\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2>0$, so $h$ is not identically zero.
     
    The variation diminishing property (cf. Def.~\ref{def: Variation deimishing}) therefore gives $Z(h)\leq V(g)$, where zeros are counted with multiplicity.
     
    On the other hand, the stationarity conditions imply that each $\vartheta_j$ is a zero of multiplicity at least two.
     
    Consequently,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        2A\leq Z(h)\leq V(g)\leq 2A.
    \end{equation*}
     
    Thus, all inequalities are in fact equalities, and the $\vartheta_j$ are the only zeros of $h$, each with multiplicity exactly two.
     
    Since the positive part of $g$ is supported on at most $A$ locations, equality $V(g)=2A$ requires the alternating sign pattern negative--positive--negative--$\cdots$--positive--negative.
     
    Thus, every location in the reduced measure must have strictly positive total weight.
     

    We next establish that $h\leq0$.
     
    Since all zeros of $h$ have multiplicity exactly two, $h$ cannot change sign.
     
    Furthermore, the stationarity conditions give $\int h\,\mathrm dP=0$, and therefore
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \int h\,\mathrm dP^*=-\int h\,\mathrm d(P-P^*)=-\|\Delta\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2<0.
    \end{equation*}
     
    It follows that $h\leq0$ everywhere.
     
    Finally, the KKT conditions give $h(x_i)=\Delta(x_i)-c\geq0$ for every particle, including those with zero individual weight.
     
    Since $h\leq0$, we must thus have $h(x_i)=0$.
     
    Since all zeros of $h$ occur at the active locations $\vartheta_1,\ldots,\vartheta_A$, every particle must coincide with one of these locations.
     
    Hence every distinct particle location is active and has positive total weight.
     
    Moreover, each particle location is a strict local maximum of $h$, and its zero has multiplicity exactly two.
     
    Thus, since $h=\Delta-c$, it follows that, for every $i=1,\ldots,N$,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta(x_i)=c, \qquad \Delta'(x_i)=0, \qquad \Delta''(x_i)<0. \qedhere
    \end{equation*}

title: Proof
body_md:
By Props.~\ref{prop: neighbourhoodmiss} and \ref{prop: MMDholebound}, there exists a constant $L>0$, depending only on $P^*$, such that every spurious stationary point satisfies $\operatorname{MMD}(P,P^*)\geq L$.
     
    In Prop.~\ref{prop: MMDFourierSplit}, choose $\nu>0$ such that $4\operatorname{erfc}(\frac{\nu}{2})<\frac{L^2}{2}$.
     
    Since the bound in Prop.~\ref{prop: Lcbound} tends to zero as $c\to0$, we can choose $\underline c>0$ such that, whenever $c\leq\underline c$, it holds that
     
    \begin{equation}
        \|\Delta\|_1\leq L\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2\operatorname{erfi}(\frac{\nu}{2})}}.
    \end{equation}
     
    By Prop.~\ref{prop: MMDFourierSplit}, this would imply $\operatorname{MMD}(P,P^*)<L$, contradicting the lower bound.
     
    Thus, every spurious stationary point must satisfy $c>\underline c$.
     
    Applying Prop.~\ref{prop: NUpperBound} then gives a finite upper bound on the number of distinct active particle locations, depending only on $P^*$.
     
    If $N$ exceeds this bound, at least two particles must share a location.
     
    By Props.~\ref{prop: unstablecollisionpoints} and \ref{prop: collisionpoints}, such configurations cannot be local minima and are unstable under the unweighted particle gradient flow.

title: Proof
body_md:
The conclusion is immediate if $x_j^\infty$ is finite or if the particles escape to opposite infinities.
     
    Otherwise, suppose that some particles escape to the same infinity while maintaining finite pairwise distances, with at least two distinct limiting locations.
     
    Consider an outermost particle with positive limiting weight within such a group.
     
    In the limit, interactions with particles outside the group vanish, while the particles at distinct locations within the group exert an outward force on the outermost particle.
     
    Since the weights are nonnegative, these contributions cannot cancel, and hence its limiting derivative cannot vanish.
     
    This contradicts the stationarity condition \eqref{cAStationary0}.

label: prop: asymptoticposweight
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop: asymptoticposweight}
Suppose we are at a spurious asymptotically stationary configuration of $F(\mathbf w,\boldsymbol{x})$.
 
Then $c>0$.
 
Moreover, if $\vartheta_i^\infty\in\{\pm\infty\}$, then $\varsigma_i^\infty=c$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By assumption, at least one particle location escapes to infinity with positive limiting weight.
     
    Let $\vartheta_i^\infty\in\{\pm\infty\}$ denote such a location.
     
    By Prop.~\ref{prop: infsep}, all other distinct locations with nonzero limiting weight are infinitely separated from it.
     
    Consequently, for the Gaussian kernel,
     
    \begin{equation*}
        \Delta_\infty(\vartheta_i^\infty)=\varsigma_i^\infty k(\vartheta_i^\infty,\vartheta_i^\infty)=\varsigma_i^\infty.
    \end{equation*}
     
    The stationarity condition \eqref{aStationarycred} therefore gives $\varsigma_i^\infty=c$.
     
    Since $\varsigma_i^\infty>0$, it follows that $c>0$.
